Pagan temples hid their most sacred objects in the inner adyton, to be seen only on special festival days when the doors were opened.

God's covenant presence, unseen in the earthly sanctuary, is revealed in heaven: his covenant faithfulness to his people is the ground of the coming judgments and of their salvation. The lightning, thunder, earthquake and hail end the trumpet series and anticipate the bowls (16:18-21), and the heavenly temple frames the next section (chapters 12-14).
The heavenly reality supersedes the earthly temple about to be destroyed in AD 70: access to God's presence is now through the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 9:11-12; Chilton).

The heavenly sanctuary from which the final judgments of the Tribulation proceed; the ark of the covenant signals that God is about to keep his covenant promises, including those made to Israel (Walvoord, Thomas).
Revelation of God's covenant presence, guaranteeing the salvation of his people at the consummation and introducing a new cycle of visions.
Lightning, rumblings, thunder, an earthquake and great hail
The Sinai storm theophany (Exodus 19:16-19), with hail added from the Egyptian plague (Exodus 9:23-24) and Joshua's battle (Joshua 10:11). The formula expands from 8:5 and anticipates 16:18-21.
The end of the trumpet series in the final theophany of judgment; the escalating formula ties together the ends of the seals (8:5), trumpets (11:19) and bowls (16:18-21).
Supports recapitulation: each series ends at the final judgment (Bauckham, Beale).
Literal phenomena in the final stage of the Tribulation, in a progressive sequence.

Revelation 11 is a key text for the pre-70 dating and preterist reading (Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell; Chilton, Days of Vengeance). The temple still stands and John measures its inner sanctuary (the faithful remnant) while the outer court and holy city are handed to the Roman armies for the 42 months of the Jewish War (AD 67-70), as Jesus foretold in Luke 21:24. The great city "where their Lord was crucified" is Jerusalem; the two witnesses are the church's witness in Jerusalem (variously identified). The seventh trumpet announces the kingdom of God, decisively established in Christ's ascension and vindicated by the judgment on Jerusalem, and continuing until the final judgment. This reading depends on the disputed pre-70 date (see the context above).

Full preterists accept the first-century reading of the temple, the 42 months and the great city, but also take the seventh trumpet as the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52, so that the resurrection, judgment of the dead and full arrival of the kingdom took place (spiritually) in AD 70 (Max King, Don Preston). This places the view outside the creeds, which confess a future bodily resurrection and final judgment; proponents reply that the time statements of the New Testament require it, while critics (including partial preterists such as Gentry) argue that it confuses a covenantal judgment with the end of history.

The chapter traces the true church through the 1,260 years of papal supremacy. Measuring the temple is the Reformation's restoration of true worship by the rule of Scripture, with the outer court representing nominal Christendom. The two witnesses are the faithful minority who testified against Rome across the centuries (Waldenses, Wycliffe, Hus); their apparent death and three-and-a-half-day exposure correspond to the suppression of dissent proclaimed at the Fifth Lateran Council (1514), and their resurrection to Luther's Reformation (1517). The earthquake and fall of a tenth of the city are often applied to the Reformation or the French Revolution, and the seventh trumpet looks to the final triumph of Christ (Elliott, Barnes).

A rebuilt temple will stand in Jerusalem during the Tribulation; it is measured while the city is trampled by Gentiles for 42 months under the Antichrist. Two literal prophets (perhaps Moses and Elijah, or Enoch and Elijah) minister for 1,260 days with miraculous powers, are killed by the Antichrist in Jerusalem, lie unburied for three and a half literal days while the world watches, and are raised and taken to heaven. A great earthquake strikes Jerusalem, and survivors acknowledge God. The seventh trumpet anticipates Christ's return to set up his literal kingdom (Walvoord, Thomas).

The temple is the church, measured (protected) in its spiritual life while its outward existence is trampled throughout the church age (the 42 months). The two witnesses are the witnessing church, in the roles of Moses and Elijah, the royal priesthood of Zechariah 4; they suffer, appear to be defeated at the end by the beast, but are raised and vindicated. The great city is the world-system in rebellion. The response of the survivors in 11:13 portrays the conversion of the nations through the church's faithful witness. The seventh trumpet is the last judgment and consummation (Hendriksen, Beale, Bauckham).

Many recent commentators blend approaches. Osborne and Ladd, for example, see a future fulfilment involving literal Jerusalem and perhaps two individual prophets, while also seeing the witnesses as models for the church's witness in every age. Bauckham and Koester stress first-century resonances (the trampled city, Nero's persecution, the imperial claims) along with the symbolic nature of the measures and the universal scope of the church's witness.

Postmillennialists emphasize that the seventh trumpet proclaims a kingdom already given to Christ at his ascension (Daniel 7:13-14; Matthew 28:18) and that the church's witness (11:13) leads to the conversion of the nations. Partial preterist postmillennialists see AD 70 as the public vindication of the kingdom, after which it grows through the gospel until the final judgment summarised in 11:18.

Amillennialists read 11:15-19 as the end of history: the seventh trumpet is the last trumpet, the consummation of the kingdom and the final judgment, parallel to the end of the seals (6:12-17) and the bowls (16:17-21). The witnesses' 1,260 days are the church age, with the beast's war on them corresponding to the final rebellion of 20:7-10 (Beale, Hendriksen, Riddlebarger).

Historic premillennialists (Ladd) see the seventh trumpet as anticipating Christ's return, after which he reigns on earth during the millennium (Revelation 20) before the final judgment; 11:15-18 compresses these stages into a single announcement. Ladd held that the passage may point to the future conversion of Israel (Romans 11:26).

Dispensational premillennialists place the chapter in the future seven-year Tribulation, which is Daniel's seventieth week, with a rebuilt temple and two literal prophets; the seventh trumpet announces Christ's return at the end of the Tribulation to establish the millennial kingdom from Jerusalem. They usually distinguish this trumpet from the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52, which they connect with a pretribulational rapture (Walvoord, Thomas).
What does the act of measuring signify in Ezekiel 40, Zechariah 2 and Amos 7? Which background best fits Revelation 11:1-2, and why?
Are the two witnesses two individuals or a symbol of the witnessing church? Weigh the clues: lampstands (Revelation 1:20), Moses and Elijah, worldwide audience (11:9).
How does the reference to the great city "where their Lord was crucified" affect the identity of the city, and how does that connect to Babylon in Revelation 17-18?
Compare 9:20-21 (no repentance after the trumpets) with 11:13 (people give glory to God after the witnesses' vindication). What does this contrast suggest about how God brings the nations to himself?
How do the millennial views interpret the seventh trumpet and the proclamation of the kingdom in Revelation 11:15? What would each say about the time of its fulfilment?
The Woman, the Dragon and the War in Heaven
The great conflict behind history: dragon, beasts and Lamb (chapters 12-14)

After the seventh trumpet, John steps back to show the spiritual war that lies behind the church's suffering. A radiant woman gives birth to a male child destined to rule the nations; a seven-headed red dragon tries to devour him, but the child is caught up to God's throne and the woman is protected in the wilderness. Michael and his angels expel the dragon, Satan, from heaven, and a heavenly hymn declares that the saints conquer him by the Lamb's blood and their testimony. Enraged and short of time, the dragon pursues the woman, fails, and turns to make war on her other children.
Two signs: the woman, the dragon and the male child
War in heaven: Michael casts out the dragon
Hymn of victory: the accuser thrown down
The dragon pursues the woman and her children

Chapter 12 opens the central section of Revelation (chapters 12-14), which most commentators regard as the book's theological core: it explains who the church's real enemy is and why believers suffer even though Christ has won. The imagery is thoroughly Jewish. It weaves together Genesis 3:15 (enmity between the serpent and the woman's seed), Joseph's dream of sun, moon and stars (Genesis 37), Zion in labour (Isaiah 26 and 66; Micah 4-5), the chaos dragon Leviathan or Rahab whom God crushes (Psalm 74; Isaiah 27 and 51), Daniel's angelic prince Michael and the 3.5-year persecution (Daniel 7, 10 and 12), and the exodus story of flight, eagles' wings, wilderness feeding and the earth swallowing enemies (Exodus 15 and 19; Numbers 16). Close parallels appear in the Qumran Thanksgiving Hymns and War Scroll and in 1 Enoch's accounts of fallen stars.

The chapter also speaks directly into the Greco-Roman world. The story of a pregnant goddess pursued by a dragon (Leto and Python, Isis and Typhon) was widely known, and Apollo, the child who slew Python, was a god Nero claimed to embody; coins of Domitian presented his deceased son as a divine child among the stars. Many scholars (Yarbro Collins, Aune, Koester) therefore read Revelation 12 as a deliberate counter-myth: the true divine child is Jesus, and the true dragon-slayer is God's Messiah, not the emperor. The chapter's date-dependent applications (the flight to Pella, the Neronic persecution, the Jewish War) are argued by preterists; the dating of Revelation (pre-70 or c. 95) is disputed and shapes how far such links are possible.
A great sign appeared in heaven

"Sign" (Greek semeion) recalls Isaiah 7:14, where the LORD gives a sign of a woman who conceives and bears a son, and the signs God worked in Egypt (Exodus 7:3; Deuteronomy 4:34). Jewish apocalypses commonly present heavenly tableaux that disclose the hidden meaning of earthly events (Daniel 7; 1 Enoch 85-90, the Animal Apocalypse).

Readers in Asia Minor knew the night sky as a book of omens: astrology was pervasive, constellations were tied to myths, and emperors advertised celestial portents (the comet after Julius Caesar's death, the sidus Iulium, appeared on coins). A woman crowned with stars and a dragon in the sky would evoke constellation imagery such as Virgo and Draco or Hydra.

This is the first of three 'signs' in heaven (12:1, 12:3, 15:1). It marks a new movement in the book: John steps behind the visible persecution to show the spiritual conflict driving it. Most interpreters agree the vision is symbolic, compressing the story of Messiah, his people and Satan into one scene; they differ on how much of it refers to specific historical events.
A woman clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars

The clearest background is Joseph's dream (Genesis 37:9-11), where sun, moon and stars bow to Joseph and are read as Jacob, Rachel and the sons of Israel; twelve stars therefore point to the twelve tribes. Israel or Zion is pictured as a woman and mother in Isaiah 54:1-6, 66:7-9, Micah 4:9-10 and Jeremiah 4:31; the beloved 'fair as the moon, bright as the sun' appears in Song of Songs 6:10. Later Jewish tradition (Testament of Naphtali 5:3-5) also links Levi, Judah and the tribes with sun, moon and stars.

Two pagan stories are widely compared. In the Greek Leto myth, the pregnant Leto is hunted by the serpent Python, is carried to safety, and gives birth to Apollo, who later kills the serpent; the Egyptian story of Isis, Horus and the red Typhon/Set is similar. Nero publicly cast himself as Apollo, so John's retelling may subvert imperial myth: the true divine child is Jesus, not the emperor. A coin of Domitian (c. 83) shows his dead infant son as a divine child seated on a globe amid seven stars, another possible point of contrast. The 'queen of heaven' and crowned goddesses (e.g. Roma, Artemis) were familiar civic images.

The woman is a corporate figure: the faithful covenant people of God from whom Messiah comes, who then continue as the persecuted community in the wilderness. Disputes centre on whether she is Israel only, the church only, or the one people of God spanning both covenants. The Marian reading (the woman as Mary) has a long Catholic history and some patristic support, but most Protestant and many Catholic commentators treat Mary at most as a secondary echo, since the woman's later flight and 'other offspring' (12:17) fit a community better than an individual.
The faithful remnant of Israel, mother of Messiah, who becomes the Jewish-Christian church that is protected while apostate Jerusalem is judged (Chilton, Gentry).
The true church, radiant with Christ's righteousness; her later flight is the faithful church's obscurity during the long era of papal dominance (Elliott, Barnes).

National Israel, from whom Christ came and who will be persecuted and protected during the future Great Tribulation; dispensationalists stress that the Genesis 37 imagery requires Israel, not the church (Walvoord, Thomas).
The one people of God in both testaments: Israel bringing forth Messiah and the church continuing as the bride under attack in every age (Hendriksen, Beale).
She was pregnant and crying out in the pain and agony of giving birth

Zion in labour is a prophetic image for the painful arrival of salvation: Isaiah 26:17-18, 66:7-9, Micah 4:9-10 and 5:3 (Israel 'gives birth' before the ruler from Bethlehem appears). A Qumran Thanksgiving Hymn (1QH 11, older numbering 1QH 3) describes a woman in agonising labour bringing forth a 'wonderful counsellor' while serpent-like forces threaten, a striking parallel. Later rabbinic texts speak of the 'birth pangs of the Messiah' (heblo shel mashiach) preceding the messianic age (b. Sanhedrin 98b, later material).
Childbirth was the most common cause of death for women in antiquity, and goddesses such as Artemis of Ephesus were invoked as protectors of women in labour.

The pains express the suffering of God's people as they wait for and bring forth the Messiah. Jesus uses similar language for the sufferings that precede the end (Matthew 24:8; John 16:21). Interpreters agree the picture is not about the physical nativity as such but about the covenant people's long travail.
A huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven royal crowns

The dragon is the chaos-monster of the Old Testament: Leviathan, the twisting serpent and 'dragon in the sea' (Isaiah 27:1), Rahab (Isaiah 51:9; Job 26:12-13), the many-headed Leviathan whose heads God crushed (Psalm 74:13-14), and Pharaoh as the great monster (tannin) lying in the Nile (Ezekiel 29:3; 32:2). Ugaritic texts already describe Lotan as a seven-headed serpent defeated by Baal, showing how ancient the image is. The ten horns come from Daniel's fourth beast (Daniel 7:7, 24).

Red was the colour of Typhon/Set in Egyptian lore (Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris), and Python and other serpents guarded or threatened divine births in Greek myth. Seven heads would later be linked to Rome's seven hills (Revelation 17:9). Diadems (diademata) were the royal headbands of Hellenistic kings, a claim to sovereignty.

The text itself names the dragon as Satan (12:9). Red suggests murderous violence (John 8:44); seven heads and crowns suggest the fullness of usurped royal power; ten horns signal great military strength, and the dragon's features are passed on to the sea beast (13:1) and the scarlet beast (17:3), showing that persecuting empires are his instruments.
Satan working through the Roman empire (seven heads as emperors or hills, ten horns as provincial or client rulers) in the first century.
Satan embodied first in pagan imperial Rome; the heads are its successive forms of government (Elliott, Barnes).
Satan, whose heads and horns anticipate the end-time empire and ten-king confederation of Revelation 17 and Daniel 7 (Walvoord).
Satan as the power behind every persecuting world-system; the numbers express completeness and might, not particular rulers (Hendriksen).
His tail swept a third of the stars from the sky, tossing them to the earth

Daniel 8:10 describes the little horn (Antiochus IV) growing to the host of heaven and throwing some of the stars to the ground; there the stars are the faithful of Israel or their angelic patrons (compare Daniel 12:3). 1 Enoch 86-88 pictures fallen angels as stars falling from heaven, and Isaiah 14:12 uses the morning star image for a fallen king.
Ancient astronomy imagined comets and meteors as stars falling or being swept away, often read as omens of disaster for rulers.

The 'third' is a partial, limited destruction, as in the trumpet judgments. Two main readings exist: the fall of angels who joined Satan's rebellion (a very old reading, connecting with 12:7-9 where the dragon has 'his angels'), or Satan's assault on God's people, following Daniel 8:10. Many commentators combine them, seeing the verse as a picture of the dragon's destructive power rather than a precise chronology.
Often taken as the original fall of angels who followed Satan, now his demonic host (Walvoord).
Following Daniel 8:10, the dragon's persecution of the saints and the apostasy he provokes, rather than a primeval fall (Beale).
Satan's attack on Israel's faithful leaders and the apostasy of first-century Israel's rulers (Chilton).
The dragon stood before the woman, ready to devour her child

Pharaoh's order to drown Israel's baby boys (Exodus 1:16-22) and Jeremiah 51:34 (Babylon as a dragon that swallowed Jerusalem) supply the pattern of the monster devouring God's people. The serpent's hostility to the woman's offspring goes back to Genesis 3:15.
In the Leto myth Python sought to kill the unborn Apollo; the motif of a tyrant threatening a royal child was standard in ancient legend.

Most readers see a compressed allusion to the whole of Satan's opposition to Messiah, with Herod's massacre of the infants at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16) as its clearest historical instance, and the cross as its climax.
A son, a male child, who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter

Isaiah 66:7 speaks of Zion giving birth to a 'male child' before her labour; Psalm 2:9 promises the anointed King that he will shepherd or break the nations with a rod of iron. Revelation applies Psalm 2 to Jesus (19:15) and shares it with the faithful (2:26-27).
Imperial propaganda celebrated the birth of heirs as the dawn of a golden age (Virgil's Fourth Eclogue was read this way), and Nero was hailed as a new Apollo.

The child is Jesus the Messiah, the son of Psalm 2. The redundant 'son, a male' (huion arsen) highlights the fulfilment of Isaiah 66:7. Almost all interpreters agree; a few historicists and others have proposed secondary referents.

Some classic historicists (e.g. Elliott) saw the birth also as the 'birth' of a Christian empire under Constantine, when the church's offspring rose to rule; most later historicists returned to Christ.
Christ himself; some dispensational writers add the church united to him, raptured before the tribulation, though Walvoord and most keep the referent to Christ.
Her child was caught up to God and to His throne

Exaltation to God's throne recalls Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13-14, where the one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive dominion. Elijah and Enoch were also taken up in Jewish tradition (2 Kings 2:11; Genesis 5:24).
Romans spoke of emperors being taken up to the gods at death (apotheosis), shown on coins and reliefs with eagles carrying the deceased emperor heavenward.

The life of Jesus is telescoped from birth to ascension: Satan's attempt to destroy him fails, and he is enthroned. The verb harpazo (snatched) stresses God's rescue. The scene implies that the cross and resurrection, though unmentioned, are Satan's defeat.
The woman fled into the wilderness, to a place prepared by God, to be nourished

The wilderness is Israel's place of both testing and divine care after the exodus, where God fed them with manna (Exodus 16; Deuteronomy 8:2-4). Elijah fled to the wilderness and was fed by ravens and an angel (1 Kings 17:2-6; 19:3-8). Hosea 2:14 promises that God will lure Israel into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her. Qumran's community deliberately withdrew to the desert to 'prepare the way' (Isaiah 40:3; 1QS 8:13-14).

Eusebius (Church History 3.5.3) records that the Jerusalem Christians, warned by an oracle, fled to Pella in the Decapolis before the siege of Jerusalem; historians debate the tradition's reliability.

The faithful community is protected and sustained by God in a time of persecution, living as pilgrims between exodus and promised land. The 'place prepared' echoes John 14:2-3 language of God's provision. Protection here is spiritual preservation, not exemption from suffering, since the dragon still makes war on her children (12:17).
The Jerusalem church's flight to Pella before AD 70 in obedience to Jesus' warning (Matthew 24:16), or more broadly the protected Jewish-Christian remnant (Chilton, Gentry).
The true church driven into obscurity (Waldenses, Albigenses and other dissenting groups) during the 1,260 years of papal supremacy (Elliott, Barnes).

A Jewish remnant fleeing at the midpoint of Daniel's seventieth week (Matthew 24:15-21); some dispensationalists suggest a refuge such as Petra (compare Isaiah 16:1-4), while others decline to name a place (Walvoord).
The church throughout the age, a pilgrim people kept and fed by God through word and sacrament while living in a hostile world (Hendriksen, Beale).
1,260 days; a time, and times, and half a time

The period comes from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7 ('a time, times and half a time'), the length of the little horn's persecution, historically tied to Antiochus IV's desecration of the temple (167-164 BC). Three and a half years was also the length of the drought in Elijah's day according to Jesus and James (Luke 4:25; James 5:17), linking it with prophetic witness and wilderness provision. Revelation uses three equivalent forms: 42 months (11:2; 13:5), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6) and time-times-half (12:14).
Half of seven, the period represents a limited, God-bounded time of persecution and protection: severe, but cut short. Debate concerns whether it is literal, a symbol, or a code for years.
A roughly three-and-a-half-year period in the first century: the Jewish War of 66-70 or the Neronic persecution from late 64 to Nero's death in June 68 (Gentry).

On the day-for-a-year principle (Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6), 1,260 years of papal ascendancy, often dated from 538 (Justinian's support of the Roman bishop) to 1798 (the pope's capture by French forces), with other start dates proposed (Barnes, Elliott).
The literal second half of Daniel's seventieth week, the Great Tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas).
The whole church age between Christ's ascension and return, seen as a short, limited time of trial in which God preserves his people (Hendriksen, Beale).
War broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon

Michael is the angelic 'great prince' who stands for Israel in Daniel 10:13, 10:21 and 12:1, where his arising coincides with an unparalleled time of distress. In 1 Enoch 20:5 he is set over the people of God, in the Qumran War Scroll (1QM 17:6-8) God exalts Michael's rule among the angels when the sons of light win, and Jude 9 shows him disputing with the devil. His name means 'Who is like God?', which the beast's worshippers parody in 13:4.
Greek myth told of wars in heaven (the Titanomachy and Gigantomachy, the latter vividly carved on the Great Altar of Pergamum, the city of 'Satan's throne' in Revelation 2:13).

Satan loses his place of access in heaven. The hymn that follows (12:10-11) connects the victory to the 'blood of the Lamb', implying that Michael's victory is the heavenly counterpart of Christ's earthly work at the cross and ascension, as in Luke 10:18 and John 12:31. The main dispute is timing: primeval, at the cross, or still future.
A future event at the midpoint of the tribulation, when Satan is finally barred from heaven and turns his fury on Israel (Walvoord, Thomas).
The heavenly side of Christ's victory at the cross and ascension; since then Satan can no longer accuse believers before God (Hendriksen, Beale).
The result of Christ's death, resurrection and ascension in the first century, leading to Satan's rage against the church and Israel up to AD 70 (Chilton, Gentry).
Classic historicists read the war as the struggle between Christianity and paganism within the Roman empire, ending when paganism was cast from the imperial throne under Constantine (Elliott).
The great dragon, that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world

The 'ancient serpent' is the tempter of Genesis 3; the Wisdom of Solomon 2:24 already identifies the serpent's envy with the devil. 'Satan' (Hebrew ha-satan, the adversary) is the prosecuting angel of Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1-2; 'devil' (diabolos, slanderer) is the Greek translation used in the Septuagint. 1 Enoch 40:7 speaks of 'satans' who accuse humans before God.

John piles up names to unmask the dragon: the deceiver from Eden, the accuser, the slanderer. Deception is his chief weapon throughout Revelation (13:14; 20:3, 8, 10), which is why the beasts work by signs and propaganda. All views agree that a personal evil power is meant.
He was hurled to the earth, and his angels with him

Isaiah 14:12-15 and Ezekiel 28:16-17 (taunts against the kings of Babylon and Tyre, long applied to Satan's fall) speak of being cast from heaven to earth. Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning (Luke 10:18) and that the ruler of this world would be 'cast out' at the cross (John 12:31).

The casting down is a defeat but also the reason for intensified persecution on earth. It explains the church's experience: Satan is beaten yet dangerous, like a wounded animal. Amillennial interpreters link it with the binding of Satan in 20:1-3 as two views of the same victory; premillennialists generally distinguish them.
Parallel to the binding of Satan in Revelation 20: both describe the curtailing of Satan's power through Christ's first coming (Hendriksen, Riddlebarger).
A distinct future event in the tribulation; the binding of Revelation 20 is later still, at Christ's return (Walvoord).
Satan's defeat at the cross begins here, but the binding of Revelation 20 is a further, future restriction at the Parousia (Ladd).
The accuser of our brothers, who accuses them day and night before our God

In Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3 the satan acts as prosecutor in God's heavenly court. Greek kategor was borrowed into later Hebrew and Aramaic as qategor, the term rabbis used for Satan as prosecutor of Israel. A later rabbinic tradition (b. Yoma 20a) observes that the numerical value of ha-satan is 364, so Satan may accuse on every day of the year except the Day of Atonement, when Israel is cleansed; this is later material but shows how naturally accusation and atonement were linked.
Roman Asia knew the role of the delator, the informer who brought accusations, sometimes against Christians, before magistrates (Pliny, Letters 10.96-97, mentions anonymous accusations).
Satan's charge against believers is silenced because Christ's sacrifice answers it (Romans 8:33-34). The hymn turns legal language into worship: the court verdict has been handed down for the saints.
Now have come the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of His Christ

The language draws on Psalm 2 (the LORD and his anointed) and Daniel 7:14, 27 (dominion given to the son of man and the saints). The hymn answers 11:15, where the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.
Acclamations of an emperor's victory (soteria, dynamis, basileia) were standard at imperial celebrations; John assigns those claims to God and his Messiah.

The 'now' marks the decisive arrival of God's reign through Christ's work. Interpreters disagree whether the 'now' is the first-century triumph of the cross (inaugurated kingdom) or an end-time moment, but the hymn's link to the Lamb's blood favours the cross for most commentators.
The kingdom has come at the ascension and will progressively triumph through the gospel in history (Chilton, Gentry).
Proleptic: the hymn celebrates the future earthly kingdom that will follow the tribulation (Walvoord).
They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony; they did not love their lives so as to shy away from death

Jewish martyr theology held that the faithful who die rather than betray the covenant win a victory and even serve God's purposes (Daniel 11:32-35; 2 Maccabees 7; 4 Maccabees 17:11-22, which presents the martyrs' deaths as a ransom and triumph over the tyrant).

'Testimony' (martyria) is courtroom vocabulary; in Roman trials, Christians' confession before the governor (as in Pliny's letters) could cost them their lives, and the word 'martyr' gradually came to mean one who dies for the faith.

The saints win not by force but by relying on Christ's atoning death and by faithful witness unto death. This redefines victory in Revelation: the Lamb and his followers conquer by suffering (5:5-6; 15:2). It is the theological centre of the chapter.
Woe to the earth and the sea; the devil has come down in great fury, knowing he has only a short time
The 'woe' recalls the three woes announced by the eagle (8:13); the intensification of evil just before God's final intervention is a common apocalyptic pattern (Daniel 12:1; 4 Ezra 5:1-12).
